extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing newspaper stories about fires, accidents, deaths/funerals, crime, weather, and sporting events — covering what to feature in leads, how to structure bodies, sourcing, language use, and legal/ethical cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of Fire (feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of the fire, if unusual or mysterious, may be featured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature the cause when it has special interest; examples include cotton whiskers and a candle causing death and destruction. If the origin is undetermined, report that fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buildings or Property (feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular buildings, if especially valuable by reason of their age, location, or cost of construction, may be features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature historically or architecturally important buildings or those with large monetary value; include estimated damage costs and reasons for significance (age, style, public value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Fire Features to Consider
rubrics_metrics.description: One may feature any one of a number of particulars: the occupants of the building, the owners, any prominent persons involved, the amount and character of the damage, the amount of insurance, how the fire was discovered, how it spread, when the alarm was given, the promptness or delay of the fire department, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any of these particulars may be featured provided it has unusual importance or interest; choose the single most newsworthy particular for the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of the Fire Story (required content)
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of the fire story may continue with such of the details enumerated in the preceding paragraphs as are not used in the lead. Somewhere in the story the extent of the damage and the amount of insurance should be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include extent of damage and amount of insurance. Add emphasis and action by quoting direct statements of eyewitnesses or persons injured (janitor account, woman's premonition, etc.) to increase interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard Against Rumors at Fires
rubrics_metrics.description: In reporting a fire, particularly a big one, the reporter should guard against the wild rumors about the extent of the loss, the number of persons injured or burned to death, the certainty of arson, etc., which usually gain currency among the spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take such stories at face value; investigate until details are accurate. If you cannot prove them true or false, omit them or record them explicitly as rumors. Maintain composure amid pandemonium so you can judge information accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accident Story Lead (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead should play up the number of lives lost or endangered, the cause of the accident, the extent of the damage or injury, the time, and the place, answering the questions who, what, when, where, why, and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any one of these may be featured according to importance. If several persons have been killed or hurt and names are obtainable, make a list of the dead and injured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accident Story Body (structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of the accident story may continue in simple chronological order, reserving unimportant details until the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chronological narration after the lead; include names, causes, and sequence of events. Reserve minor details for the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playing up Probable Cause to Promote Follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: It is worth noting the shrewdness with which the reporter plays up the probable cause of the accident, adding to the actual facts and promising possible further developments in tomorrow's paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caution — emphasize likely causes when justified and use them to signal continuing coverage, but avoid speculation presented as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather Story: match form to severity
rubrics_metrics.description: The weather takes its place in the accident division because of its frequent harmful effects. Usually a story about the weather depends for its value largely on the felicity of its language, though when there has been severe atmospheric disturbance resulting in loss of life, destruction of property, or delayed traffic, a simple narrative of events is sufficient to hold the reader's attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For routine forecasts, exert effort to present facts originally and attractively; for severe events, use straightforward narrative detailing effects and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deaths and Funerals: tone and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Most newspapers require their reporters to confine themselves to bare statements of facts concerning the dead person's life, because attempting to write sympathetically risks bathos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid melodrama and editorializing; be factual and dignified to meet surviving friends' expectations without descending into bathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of Death Stories (required facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are a few facts which all death stories should contain: the person's name, age, street address, and position or business should normally be included in the lead, with possibly a statement of the cause of his death. The duration of his illness, names of surviving relatives, marriage date and wife's maiden name (if married), length of residence in the city, birthplace and occasion of settlement, holdings if wealthy, and funeral details (pallbearers, time/place, officiating minister, place of burial) may follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order may vary, but these particulars should be present. For prominent persons, include career highlights and significant contributions; close with funeral arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining Information for Death Stories (sourcing)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a person of little prominence, go first to the undertaker who will have funeral details and facts the family wishes public; additional facts may be had from county/state directories, city directories, old residents, or Who's Who volumes for prominent persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a morgue write-up, bridge naturally between new and old material so the reader does not suspect a patched story; avoid incoherent stitching of wire copy and archive material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime Lead (what to feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the lead to a crime story, one may feature either the names of the persons involved, the number of lives lost or endangered, the motive of the criminal, the nature of the crime, clues leading to the identification and arrest of the criminal, possible effects of the crime, or even public sentiment resulting from the deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the most newsworthy feature for the lead; names of persons involved are often played up. Be selective and proportionate to importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of the Crime Story (structure and emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of the crime story follows the lead in a simple chronological narration of events. Interest may be added by quoting direct statements from persons immediately connected with the crime — how it felt to be held up, how the robber gained entrance, how the bandits escaped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In burglaries/robberies include value of stolen goods and any ingenious devices used. Give due emphasis to motive unless the purpose is obvious; investigate motives rather than accepting them at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution Against Libel in Crime Reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: According to American law, a person suspected of or charged with crime is innocent until proved guilty. In writing crime stories the reporter must be doubly careful to have a supposed criminal merely 'suspected' or 'alleged' or 'said by the police' rather than declared guilty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cautious wording ('suspected', 'alleged', 'said by the police'), present the side of the supposed malefactor, avoid appeals to readers (leave that to editorial writers), and aim to present mere facts to avoid irreparable injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: permissive use of slang with clarity constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: In writing stories of athletic meets and games the reporter will find that in matters of language he has almost complete freedom; slang is freely used because timeliness and 'punch' matter to fans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slang can brighten sporting stories but ensure every detail remains clear to fans; avoid overdoing slang — better none than a story choked with jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four Kinds of Sporting Stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Sporting news stories are of four kinds: (1) those dealing with athletic events before their occurrence; (2) those reporting the events; (3) those analyzing and explaining the events and their results; and (4) those dealing with the sport in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each kind according to its needs (previews, running accounts, analysis/columns, and broader features).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports Lead (what to feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The feature most frequently played up is the final result, with additional mention of the causes of victory or defeat, the equality or inequality of the opposing players, and any important incidents. Always give the names of the teams, the time, and the place, and include the score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, feature the result/score; leads are often written last to allow inclusion of final results after a running account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of Teams and Score in Sports Leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost as frequent is the featuring of the names of the opposing teams, with the final score included at the end of the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When featuring team names, still include the final score to inform readers immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of Victory or Defeat (sports feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of a team's victory or defeat often makes an effective feature for the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain contributing factors (e.g., inability to hit, poor fielding) succinctly and link them to the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual Players (sports feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stellar work by individual players — even poor work when responsible for the loss — often makes necessary the featuring of their names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name standout performers or those whose mistakes decided the contest; include concrete examples of pivotal plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Sports Lead Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the kind of weather, the condition of the grounds, the size of the crowd, or the effect of the play on the crowd may be featured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these features to color the lead; note that the final score should nevertheless always be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of the Sports Story (content options)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies of stories reporting athletic contests vary: with limited space include lineup, names of officials, mention of those starring or playing poorly, when and how scoring was made, the condition of the field and the weather, and the size of the crowd. Fuller reports add important plays chronologically; detailed accounts give all plays in chronological order after a summarizing lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For major events, sporting editors may assign two reporters (one general account, one detailed). The general summary writer compiles summarizing figures (attendance and receipts) and comparisons with previous events.
